articles.title: Do algorithmic information environments mark the end of media effects research?
articles.authors: Isabelle Freiling, Jakob Ohme, Isabel I Villanueva, Dietram A Scheufele
articles.abstract: Algorithmically curated information environments are beginning to challenge both long-standing notions of what media effects look like and our ability to study them directly. Algorithmic curation and microtargeting of content based on users’ behavioral and digital trace data pose conceptual as well as methodological challenges to our understanding of communication effects. These challenges increasingly introduce significant distortions to our field’s current ability to transparently and systematically iterate between theory and empirical testing. In this article, we provide a blueprint for how a systematic, empirical rethinking, and testing of communication effects theory can look like in an era of what we call preference-based information ecologies (PBIEs). Specifically, we discuss 9 current challenges to theorizing that are conceptual and methodological in nature and discuss necessary field developments to address and overcome these challenges. We identify 4 major agenda items that our field must tackle in order to position itself for a future in which all communication processes occur in some variant of PBIEs.

articles.title: A systematic review of the deficit model and call for empowerment toward informed publics
articles.authors: Aart van Stekelenburg, Gabi Schaap, Harm Veling, Moniek Buijzen, Marieke L Fransen
articles.abstract: The deficit model, assuming some deficit in the public relevant to science, is one of the most influential and discussed models of science communication. Despite its popularity, the literature appears to lack a unified definition and heavily criticizes the model. The first aim of the current work is to create clarity on the deficit model and as such address the controversy surrounding it. We distill a definition of the deficit model through a systematic review of all works in which the model plays a key role (k = 178). The results demonstrate that there is no such thing as the deficit model. Instead, descriptions take many forms, making the model too broad and imprecise to test empirically or apply in practice. The second aim is to investigate if we can build on the deficit model to create a more specific and testable model for scientific information dissemination. To that end, we introduce a new model that addresses criticism of the deficit model, focuses on informing publics, and is empirically testable. This empowerment model of informed publics identifies publics not as deficient, but as active agents that should be informed and empowered. Finally, we set out areas of research for science communication scholars investigating how to inform publics.

articles.title: Structural Media Capture: Rethinking media in the Global South
articles.authors: Bouziane Zaid
articles.abstract: This article develops Structural Media Capture (SMC) as a theoretical framework for rethinking media power in postcolonial settings. Challenging the universalization of liberal-democratic normative models of the press, it advances a de-Westernizing approach that situates media development within historically specific institutional trajectories rather than universal ideals. The article theorizes from Morocco, with comparative reference to the Arab media context, and identifies three overlapping configurations of capture: post-independence state consolidation, market-driven economic dependency, and platform-based infrastructural control. Its central claim is that these configurations interact and accumulate, producing a layered architecture of media constraint. SMC does more than aggregate accounts of political, economic, or platform domination. It reconceptualizes media capture as a path-dependent and multi-level formation through which older regimes of control persist within newer institutional arrangements. In doing so, the article offers a historically grounded grammar for comparative media theory and proposes a framework for analysis across Global South contexts.

articles.title: Political protest seeks corporate sponsor: Rethinking Big Tech, youth agency, and the reordering of power from Nigeria
articles.authors: Jaana Serres
articles.abstract: This article examines how Big Tech became absorbed into local moral and political frameworks in Nigeria, Africa’s largest digital market, where the majority of the population is under 20. It maps Nigeria’s evolving platform regulations and situates recent state interventions within broader socio-economic tensions, culminating in the youth protest movement #EndSARS. The article traces how #EndSARS emerged from the entertainment industry and carried forward the organizational logic and political ethos of the globally connected, youth-led Afrobeats industry. It shows how the digital platforms that recently enabled Afrobeats’ rise not only served as infrastructure for organization and amplification, but were also called upon to actively provide corporate support against government oppression. Corporate sponsorship of the protest was simultaneously an aspirational horizon for protesters, a limited material reality through tech companies’ involvement, and a perceived threat for the political establishment. With this case study, the article intervenes in the academic consensus that conceptualizes Big Tech companies as engines of neocolonialism to draw attention to the ambivalence of emic reinterpretations, especially in contexts of generational and ethno-regional tensions. It underscores the need to understand the local dynamics that shape platforms’ symbolic power, as they can pose obstacles to effective regulation.

articles.title: Relationship Between Cyberbullying and Social Anxiety, School Refusal, and Academic Goals in Adolescents
articles.authors: Elizabeth Cañas, María Carmen Martínez-Monteagudo, Beatriz Delgado, Esther Rubio, David Aparisi
articles.abstract: Examining the associations between cyberbullying involvement and psychoeducational factors may contribute to a better understanding of adolescents’ experiences in online peer contexts. The aim of this study was to examine the associations between cyberbullying involvement, considering the roles of cybervictim, cyberaggressor, and cyberbystander, and three psychoeducational constructs: social anxiety, school refusal, and academic goals. A total of 1,412 Spanish secondary and upper-secondary school students aged 12–18 years ( M = 14.36, SD = 1.65) completed a battery of questionnaires assessing cyberbullying, social anxiety, school refusal, and academic goals. Three independent binary logistic regression models were conducted, one for each cyberbullying role, using the psychoeducational dimensions as predictors. The findings showed that the associations varied according to both the psychoeducational dimension and the cyberbullying role. In particular, Discomfort and avoidance in social situations in general was positively associated with cybervictimization, cyberaggression, and cyberbystanding, whereas other dimensions of social anxiety showed negative associations with some roles. Avoidance of stimuli or situations related to the school context was positively associated with the three cyberbullying roles. Learning and Achievement goals were negatively associated with cybervictimization, cyberaggression, and cyberbystanding, whereas Social reinforcement goals were positively associated with cyberaggression. These findings highlight the multidimensional nature of the associations between psychoeducational factors and cyberbullying involvement and support the consideration of individual and educational variables in the design of prevention and intervention strategies during adolescence.

articles.title: The dual impact of technostress on social networking services users' lurking intention: a post-adoption regret perspective
articles.authors: Xiaodan Liu, Mengyao Zhao, Chao Su
articles.abstract: Purpose Social networking services provide users with effective tools to connect with others and manage increasingly large social networks. However, users often face a “connectivity paradox,” where the advantages of network expansion are offset by the role stress induced by these technologies. To address this paradox, this study employed the holistic technostress model to investigate the dual effects of technostress on users' lurking intention through the lens of perceived post-adoption regret. Design/methodology/approach Survey data were collected from 641 Chinese WeChat users. The model and hypotheses testing were conducted using SmartPLS 4.0. Findings The findings revealed that challenge technostressors (i.e. social interaction) reduce lurking intention by strengthening perceived tie strength, while hindrance technostressors (i.e. role stress) increase lurking intention by intensifying perceived impression management dissatisfaction. Furthermore, perceived impression management dissatisfaction can heighten perceived post-adoption regret, further amplifying lurking intention. Although perceived tie strength can partially alleviate lurking intention, strong perceived tie strength may paradoxically exacerbate them by increasing perceived post-adoption regret. Originality/value Anchored in the holistic technostress model, this study explores the impacts of challenge and hindrance technostress on users' lurking intention and uncovers the dual effects of social networking services (SNS) technological affordances in the post-adoption stage. Drawing on a role-based theoretical lens, this research further elucidates the underexamined “relationship-maintenance paradox” in the SNS context. By integrating the construct of post-adoption regret, the present study reconceptualizes lurking as a maladaptive coping strategy, which challenges the mainstream scholarly view that frames lurking as a normative and benign user behavior. This theoretical reframing offers an in-depth insight into lurking behaviors, clarifying that such behaviors essentially stem from users' negative emotional responses to role-related technostress.

articles.title: The double-edged sword of proactive GenAI: how it shapes user usage intention
articles.authors: Baozhou Lu, Jun Gao, Chengwei Li
articles.abstract: Purpose With the emergence of generative AI (GenAI), proactive services that initiate actions on behalf of users without explicit prompts are becoming increasingly prevalent. Although such services can enhance human-AI interaction, emerging evidence suggests that GenAI proactivity may also elicit adverse user reactions. To reconcile these mixed findings, this research examines why and when GenAI's proactive services positively and negatively influence users' usage intention. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on mind perception theory, we develop a dual-pathway model proposing that increased proactivity simultaneously enhances perceived agency and diminishes perceived control. We further propose that task type (hedonic vs. utilitarian) determines the relative dominance of these two pathways. We test these predictions through two scenario-based experiments. Study 1 examines the dual-pathway model in a health assistant context, whereas Study 2 investigates the moderating role of task type in a shopping assistant context. Findings Study 1 demonstrates that high (vs. low) proactivity simultaneously increases perceived agency and reduces perceived control. Study 2 shows that task type moderates these effects: for the hedonic task, the positive pathway through perceived agency dominates, making high proactivity more favorable; for the utilitarian task, the negative pathway through perceived control prevails, making low proactivity more preferred. Originality/value This research advances the literature on GenAI's proactive services by demonstrating that their double-edged effects operate through parallel enabling and constraining pathways. We also extend mind perception theory by revealing the psychological costs of agency attribution. Practically, the findings offer actionable insights for firms seeking to tailor GenAI functionalities to enhance user experience and foster usage across diverse digital business contexts.

articles.title: Do good chat groups make good neighbors? Continuity and change of norms in neighbor relations under digital co-presence
articles.authors: Emilija Gagrčin, Olga Pasitselska
articles.abstract: Based on interviews with urban residents in Germany and Israel, this study examines how residential instant messaging groups (e.g., WhatsApp, Telegram) reshape the norms of “good neighboring”: reciprocity, distance, and speaking out. Drawing on Blokland’s public familiarity framework and Rosenblum’s theorizing of neighborly norms, we ask how digital co-presence transforms the relational conditions of neighboring and how these norms are negotiated within residential chat groups. We show that messenger groups lower the threshold for mutual support but introduce tensions through persistent mutual awareness, which are thenresolved through norm negotiation. Extending the public familiarity framework, we identify a complementary axis of performativity–discretion that manifests through norm negotiation. Residents calibrate between engagement and restraint, enacting “good enough” neighboring within the double-bounded constraints of a building and a chat group. We contribute to research on digitally mediated neighborhood communication by showing how urban dwellers achieve pragmatic coexistence through calibrated visibility.

articles.title: Context, script, cue: understanding human–AI intimate relationships
articles.authors: Fan Yang, Meiling Du, Ningxin Li, Qing Yan
articles.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into the intimate sphere of human relationships presents a profound challenge to traditional understanding of intimacy, necessitating a critical examination of this technology’s extension into a domain that has always been viewed as deeply human. Through in-depth semi-structured interviews (N = 23), this study examines how human–AI intimate relationships develop in Chinese society at the intersection of traditions and modernization. A three-pronged Context-Script-Cue (CSC) framework emerges, capturing how users navigate emotional investment alongside the artificial nature of AI. By empirically examining how users engage in human–AI intimate relationships, this study offers the new CSC framework for understanding the development of human–AI intimate relationships.

articles.title: A comparative test of the protection motivation theory: active and passive privacy protection in Brazil, Germany, the United States, and Vietnam
articles.authors: Yannic Meier, Laurent H Wang, Nicole C Krämer, Miriam J Metzger
articles.abstract: Online companies surveil users around the world for commercial purposes. We advance protection motivation theory (PMT), by categorizing user responses to surveillance as either active or passive (i.e., self-inhibition) privacy protection behavior, integrating privacy literacy overconfidence, and exploring privacy resignation as a moderator. Finally, we adopt a comparative lens by investigating protection behavior in four national contexts: Brazil, Germany, the United States, and Vietnam. Results of an online survey (Ntotal = 2,092) show that perceiving surveillance as privacy threat was not consistently associated with active protection behavior. Rather, self-inhibition was a more likely response to surveillance which may have detrimental consequences for both individuals and societies. Across countries, perceived effectiveness of active protection positively relates to both forms of protection while active protection does not prevent self-inhibition. Interestingly, privacy resignation may not always impede protection. In summary, not all aspects of PMT are generalizable when using a culturally diverse sample.

articles.title: Different Gameplay Styles, Different Psychological Needs – Linking Relatedness to Behavioral Indicators of Relational Social Influence
articles.authors: Ji Ye Kim, Dmitri Williams, Donggyu Kim, Siyi Zhou, Zituo Wang, Aimei Yang
articles.abstract: Abstract: As Massively Multiplayer Online Games (MMOGs) grow in popularity and complexity, understanding how gameplay styles relate to players’ psychological needs is increasingly important. Grounded in Self-Determination Theory, this study examines the associations between competence, autonomy, and relatedness and two dominant gameplay styles: achievement-oriented gameplay (AOG) and social-oriented gameplay (SOG). Given that relational influence provides an important context in which relatedness is enacted and sustained, we incorporate two interaction-based behavioral indicators – Social Value and Receptivity – as behavior-based measures of relational social influence. Using Sky: Children of the Light, we integrated large-scale behavioral data with survey responses. Structural equation modeling revealed that AOG was positively associated with competence and autonomy but negatively associated with relatedness and behavior-based relational influence, whereas SOG showed the opposite pattern, with parallel directional effects observed across relatedness and behavioral indicators of relational influence. A significant negative residual correlation was also observed between AOG and SOG. The results show that psychological need satisfaction differs across players’ gameplay orientations and highlight relatedness as a dynamic process shaped through ongoing interaction.

articles.title: Mapping Out the Context
articles.authors: Bingjie Liu, Andrew Gambino, Lewen Wei
articles.abstract: Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can write humanlike, context-aware messages and thus can aid individuals in their communication with others. Existing research suggests that using GenAI may be regarded as inappropriate or undesirable in certain interpersonal contexts, but acceptable in others. Yet, few studies have articulated the reasons underlying such context-dependent preferences. Taking a functional approach, we conducted an online survey ( N = 542) to explore how GenAI use might depend on an individual’s goals in interpersonal communication and to unravel the reasons why an individual may or may not use GenAI in specific contexts. Among the participants who had used GenAI in their interpersonal communication with others ( n = 240), we found that GenAI was most often used for goals of information and resource exchange. When message production for a goal requires more of one’s subjective experience (e.g., providing emotional support, showing others who you are), individuals are less likely to use GenAI in such contexts. Other contextual factors, including whether message production for a goal is difficult and whether it requires objectivity or human knowledge, were not found to predict GenAI use. These findings contribute to the theories and research in human–AI interaction and message production, while also informing the future design of human-centered AI.

articles.title: Level Up Your Mood – Mood Repair Effects of Hedonic Versus Eudaimonic Video Games
articles.authors: Gary L. Wagener, André Melzer
articles.abstract: Abstract: Current research emphasizes the therapeutic potential of hedonic video games (VGs), designed for fun and entertainment, which, for example, reduce anxiety primarily through psychological detachment. However, eudaimonic experiences of deeper emotional engagement and meaning may have even stronger therapeutic effects. In this lab experiment ( N = 95), we compared hedonic and eudaimonic VG experiences with a non-gaming control group (jigsaw puzzling) to reduce anxiety and promote relaxation. Anxiety was induced with an autobiographical recall task. Next, participants were randomly assigned to their respective activity. The anxiety levels, self-reported relaxation, and physiological relaxation (heart rate variability) were measured throughout the entire time. Both game types reduced anxiety and increased relaxation, but only the eudaimonic game led to prolonged physiological relaxation. In contrast, jigsaw puzzling did not reduce anxiety and was linked to greater stress responses. These findings highlight the therapeutic value of eudaimonic VGs, warranting further investigation through longitudinal studies.

articles.title: How Online Dating Motivations and Social Networks Affect Warranting Value and Interpersonal Impressions
articles.authors: Megan A. Vendemia
articles.abstract: Abstract: Popular online dating platforms feature self-authored profiles in which users can indicate their relational goals and interests. The ability to easily modify self-generated information raises questions about whether online daters are who they say they are offline. Informed by warranting theory, this experiment examined how online daters’ relational motivations and connections to social networks affect viewers’ authenticity judgments and interpersonal impressions. Results revealed that romantic relationship motives heightened viewers’ anticipated future interaction beliefs, which in turn, bolstered online daters’ perceived authenticity, trustworthiness, and goodwill. Results also demonstrated that connections to online daters’ broader social networks reduced relational uncertainty. Implications for warranting theory and online daters’ profile construction are discussed.

articles.title: Is Information Verification Just a Matter of Intellectual Humility?
articles.authors: Carmela Sportelli, Paolo Giovanni Cicirelli, Giuseppe Corbelli, Marinella Paciello, Francesca D’Errico
articles.abstract: Abstract: Adolescents can be vulnerable to misinformation, facing the daily challenge of assessing false, inaccurate, or misleading news. Understanding the psychological processes contributing to this vulnerability is crucial for enhancing their information verification skills. Previous research has established a positive association between intellectual humility – the acknowledgment of the fallibility of one’s own beliefs – and the intention to verify misleading content. However, the underlying process through which it occurs remains underexplored. Intellectual humility may also be linked to moral disengagement: individuals characterized by an awareness of their own fallibility can be less inclined to rely on moral disengagement mechanisms, which serve as self-serving defensive justifications used to preserve a positive self-image when faced with moral transgressions, thereby being more likely to engage in rightful online behaviors. Therefore, our research aims to test the relationship between intellectual humility and the intention to verify online content, investigating the mediating role of moral disengagement. The study, conducted with 380 Italian adolescents ( M = 14.43, SD = 0.74), utilized a conversational web app to measure the variables of interest. The results show that moral disengagement fully mediates the relationship between intellectual humility and the intention to verify the information. This highlights the importance of fostering metacognitive abilities, such as self-reflection and the capacity to reconsider one’s own perspective, in promoting media literacy. These findings suggest that interventions aimed at enhancing intellectual humility may reduce moral disengagement toward fake news and promote more responsible online behavior. Limitations and directions for future research are also discussed.

articles.title: Media Use as an Avenue to Political Identity in an Authoritarian Context?
articles.authors: Özen Odağ, Elif Bouthiller, Esma Wieacker, Nidal Toman
articles.abstract: Abstract: The current exploratory interview study investigates the link between media use and political identity formation in an authoritarian regime context – Turkey. It aims to find out how emerging adults achieve identity exploration and commitment in a country that is characterized by violations of civil liberties and human rights infringements. In such contexts, the political identity development of emerging adults is likely to draw on alternative, non-conventional forms of engagement such as media use. But the complex relationship between political identity development and media use in emerging adults is so far understudied. In the current study, semi-structured interviews were carried out with a purposeful sample of N = 22 emerging adults and subjected to an inductive coding procedure. Findings reveal four pathways of identity exploration and commitment through media, especially social and entertainment media, displaying the highly agentic nature of identity formation: (1) Discovering uncharted paths and authenticity in safe spaces; (2) Oscillating between approach and reproach; (3) Issue-based personalized commitment embedded in lived experience; (4) Validating one’s views – disengaging from conventional politics. In Turkey, emerging adults resort to alternative covert spaces and endorse non-conventional exploration and commitment activities within social media, entertainment media, their social networks, as well as the arts, forming oppositional political identities driven by lived experience.

articles.title: Friendship as Method: A Psychobiography of Audre Lorde and Pat Parker
articles.authors: Rashmi Joshi, Rajni Singh
articles.abstract: This paper centers friendship as a meaning-making tool in exploring the entwined subjectivities of two prominent feminist writers, Audre Lorde and Pat Parker. Primarily relying on their letters to each other written between 1974 and 1989 and the poems written for/about the other, the paper attempts to situate friendship as a feminist practice helpful in (re)defining one’s self-concept against societal strictures. Utilizing the psychobiographical method and drawing on Black feminist theories of affection and feminist psychoanalytical theories of women’s friendships, the paper establishes the importance of friendships as sites of self-disclosure, affirmation, validation and recognition, especially for people from marginalized social identities who have been denied visibility and voice. The paper concludes that the letters of Audre Lorde and Pat Parker are the private spaces where the two reflect on their sense of being, their identity, draw comfort from their connection, and develop survival mechanism by resisting gendered racial discrimination. These friendship letters not only serve as spaces of identity formation but also as spaces of healing.

articles.title: Loneliness Across Borders: A Cross-Sectional Study of Young Adults in Germany and Japan
articles.authors: Theresa von Pikarski, Yuka Ozaki, Maike Luhmann
articles.abstract: Despite growing evidence that loneliness is a global public health concern, much of the existing research remains concentrated in specific cultural contexts, limiting our understanding of how loneliness manifests across societies. This research explores cross-cultural variations of loneliness and its relations with life satisfaction and health-related behaviors among young adults in Germany and Japan. In a cross-sectional online study with N = 920 participants (340 from Germany, 580 from Japan), aged 18–30 years, significant differences were observed between the two samples, with the Japanese group reporting lower loneliness scores, while the German group showed higher life satisfaction and health behavior scores. Contrary to expectations, results indicated that the negative association between loneliness and both life satisfaction and health-related behaviors was not significantly moderated by culture. Similar trends emerged regarding the sociodemographic groups that were more likely to report higher loneliness scores in both countries, suggesting shared risk factors for loneliness across cultures. These findings highlight the importance of cross-cultural studies in loneliness research, especially for diverse cultural contexts beyond Western populations.

articles.title: Authoritative Yet Conditionally Cohesive: The Cohesion Dynamics of Journalistic (Non-) Authority on Chinese TikTok (Douyin)
articles.authors: Peng Xiao, Wen Shi, Yangkun Huang
articles.abstract: The rise of algorithmic curation challenges the traditional authority of journalism. Focusing on Douyin, this study employed agent-based testing and temporal network analysis to examine how recommendation systems generate network cohesion around Chinese state and non-state media. Results revealed that state media’s cohesive power stemmed from news, whereas cohesion around non-state media was sustained by non-news content. However, for both media types, the cohesion generated by news showed a significant decline over time, and this trend varied by topic. These findings suggest that, beyond mere institutional status, strategic content adaptation is fundamental to building network cohesion in algorithmic environments.

articles.title: Scientific Watchdog Journalism in Latin America: A Challenge of Broken Mirrors
articles.authors: Aleida Rueda
articles.abstract: The watchdog role of science journalism, as a way of revealing wrongdoings in science-driven enterprises, is a recent and rather invisible practice in Latin America. From my 20 years as a practitioner, this commentary explores some structural causes of this phenomenon: insufficient training opportunities in science journalism; a weak perspective of the watchdog role; a cheerleader posture by the media towards science; symbolic and political links between media owners and scientific elites; and the vulnerable position of journalists due to fragile incomes, which compromises independence and critical thinking. I also underline a further watchdog role: to investigate, expose, and warn society about the misuses and abuses of scientific methods, processes, outcomes, and authority in the public domain. In this role, the watchdog journalist verifies scientific arguments invoked to make decisions. Lastly, I relate successful instances of watchdog science journalism in the region for the social evaluation of scientific knowledge and its impact on urgent Global South problems.

articles.title: Beyond Amplifiers and Watchdogs: Rethinking Institutional Science Communication–Journalism Relations in Hybrid Media Ecosystems
articles.authors: Marina Joubert, Lars Guenther, Brian Lin, Luisa Massarani, Pampa Garcia Molina, Nora Bär
articles.abstract: Contemporary science communication increasingly unfolds within hybrid media ecosystems where scientists, institutional communicators, journalists, and audiences interact under rapidly changing conditions. In these ecosystems, universities and other research organisations have become highly visible communicative actors, supported by growing investments in strategic science communication. At the same time, science journalism faces economic precarity, shrinking newsroom capacity, and growing reliance on institutional sources. These developments have fuelled long-standing debates about hype, churnalism, and the erosion of journalism’s watchdog function, often framed as ethical or professional failings. However, these tensions between institutional science communicators and science journalists can also be seen as the structural consequences of contemporary science communication rather than as interpersonal conflicts or normative shortcomings. We conceptualise this relationship through two analytical lenses. A high-tension perspective foregrounds risks to journalistic independence, critical scrutiny, the watchdog role, and public trust under conditions of media asymmetry and the expansion of institutional authority over the public communication of science. A low-tension perspective highlights functional interdependence, role complementarity, and the ways institutional communication can enable science journalism in constrained media environments. Rather than treating these perspectives as competing accounts, we use them to illuminate different normative stakes within the same ecosystem. We thus propose a framework for constructive interdependence that acknowledges blurred boundaries and role overlap while actively protecting the integrity of independent scrutiny, and argue that safeguarding journalism’s watchdog role should be understood as a shared responsibility across communicators, institutions, and intermediaries. While we wrote this piece primarily for science communication scholars, we hope that the proposed framework offers science journalists, institutional science communicators, and research funders four concrete principles for protecting independent scrutiny as science communication ecosystems continue to change.

articles.title: Threat and Remedy: AI’s Technological and Normative Role in Democratic Discourse and Counter Speech
articles.authors: Diana Rieger, Mario Haim
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has fundamentally transformed online discourse, serving simultaneously as a source of and a potential solution to threats to democracy. This article conceptually examines AI’s multifaceted role in digital public spheres, beginning with an analysis of how AI shapes democratic processes online, ranging from information curation and political participation to dialogue facilitation and the construction of epistemic infrastructures. We identify several key risks: AI amplifies harmful content through automated content generation, coordinated manipulation, and the algorithmic mainstreaming of borderline content that often evades traditional detection systems. Within this broader democratic context, we position counter speech as a critical intervention strategy and examine both reactive measures (e.g., automated detection and content moderation) and proactive approaches (e.g., prebunking, algorithmic downranking, friction design, and AI-mediated dialogue). We argue that effective counter speech increasingly relies on human–AI collaboration, where AI supports human counter speakers with factual resources, emotional scaffolding, and scalability, while human actors preserve the authenticity and agency that make counter speech normatively meaningful. However, realizing the potential of such collaboration requires moving beyond technological fixes toward democratically legitimated governance structures. Drawing on examples from Wikipedia and decentralized platforms, we demonstrate how transparent and participatory institutional arrangements can foster more resilient discourse environments. We conclude that societies can harness AI’s democratic potential while mitigating its risks only by proactively establishing legitimate deliberative processes grounded in broadly shared discourse norms.

articles.title: Inequality Within the Mobile System: Understanding the Third-Level Digital Divide Through Adverse Digital Incorporation in Rural China
articles.authors: Jingke Lin, Jianjie Tao
articles.abstract: As mobile media rapidly expand in the rural Global South, digital divide research is shifting from an exclusion-based to an inclusion-based perspective. Drawing on Heeks’ “adverse digital incorporation” framework and ethnographic fieldwork in rural China, this article conceptualizes the third-level digital divide, which refers to the unequal outcomes and disparate dividends derived from information and communication technologies, as the unequal extraction of value resulting from power imbalances within the mobile system. The study reveals that this adverse incorporation constitutes two closed loops of value inequality. On the one hand, smartphones break spatiotemporal boundaries to extract value through the commodification of private time, legibility and labor control, and risk-cost shifting. On the other hand, while rural residents employ strategic digital disconnection as a form of everyday resistance, which results in marginalization and reinforces value inequality. Consequently, it is essential to go beyond technical provision to enable rural residents to transform from passive content consumers into active value producers and to rebalance power within the mobile system.

articles.title: Ambivalent algorithms, fragile connectedness: How algorithm awareness facets shape responsiveness and insensitivity on TikTok
articles.authors: Dragoș M. Obreja
articles.abstract: This study examines how distinct facets of algorithm awareness are associated with perceived algorithm responsiveness (PAR), perceived algorithm insensitivity (PAI), and social connectedness on TikTok. I draw on the algorithm responsiveness process and also treat algorithm awareness as four distinct dimensions (content filtering, automated decision‑making, human–algorithm interplay (HAI), ethical concerns) to examine how each dimension is differentially associated with PAR and PAI and, in turn, with feelings of inclusion and belonging. Using survey data from 305 TikTok users and structural equation modeling, I show that user‑agency‑oriented dimensions, particularly filtering and HAI, are indirectly associated with connectedness via higher responsiveness and lower insensitivity. By contrast, automation operates as an ambivalent structure: it boosts responsiveness yet is negatively associated with connectedness, marking a boundary condition for personalization. Platforms should pair automation disclosures with clearer user recourse, traceable feedback, and human review in high-stakes contexts.

articles.title: The year is a dropdown menu: Platformed provenance and the viral afterlives of AI-generated retro music
articles.authors: Matilde Catanese
articles.abstract: This article examines how generative AI media becomes believable and shareable when it is packaged as a rediscovered archive and distributed through commercial platforms. Drawing on multi-sited digital ethnography, targeted platform walkthroughs, and cross-platform trace analysis of a viral “lost song” circulating in Italy in 2025, I show how listeners in this case mobilized sonic cues and platform metadata, including release dates and credits, as practical evidence. I use metadata realism to describe everyday reliance on database fields as documentary testimony, and provenance play for situated practices of verification and narration through which people negotiate synthetic pasts. After public debunking, circulation continued through humorous and artistic reframings, while verification itself became part of the artifact’s social life. The analysis foregrounds platformed provenance and considers what the case implies for synthetic media governance and content credentials.

articles.title: News for connection, status and belonging: Exploring the social currency of local news
articles.authors: Jee Young Lee, Sora Park, Janet Fulton
articles.abstract: This paper explores the perception of social currency as a distinct value within local news consumption among audiences. Social currency refers to the value individuals derive from engaging with and sharing news content within their social networks, allowing them to connect, express identity and signal awareness. Drawing on a large-scale mixed-methods study of local news audiences in Australia (survey: n = 7919; interviews and focus groups: n = 84), this study operationalised key dimensions of social currency using factor analysis. The findings confirm that social currency is a separate and measurable construct, distinct from traditional news motivations. It is significantly higher among younger people, men, urban residents and those from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds, reflecting how news consumption intersects with social interaction, identity expression and symbolic practices of everyday life.

articles.title: Testing the Extrinsic Convergent Validity of Relationship Quality Constructs
articles.authors: Charlotte A. Sudduth, Jeffry A. Simpson, Alexander J. Rothman
articles.abstract: Relationship scientists have developed a rich array of constructs to describe the quality of relationships. Yet, questions have emerged regarding the validity of these constructs. Building on these questions, we examine the validity of a set of core constructs in relationship science. Specifically, we use extrinsic convergent validity testing to assess the extent to which the six components of the perceived relationship quality components measure (PRQC) represent distinct constructs in predicting self‐reported behavior within romantic relationships. Across one between‐subjects study ( N = 601) and one within‐subjects study ( N = 603), we used multiple indices of heterogeneity, structural equation modeling, and factor analysis to demonstrate the utility of extrinsic convergent validity testing and illustrate that some components of the PRQC appear to uniquely predict relationship behavior, whereas others may not. Implications and future directions are discussed, with particular emphasis placed on refining both measurement and theory practices.

articles.title: Empathy in the Context of Sibling Relationships: A Meta‐Analysis and Systematic Review
articles.authors: Annika L. Klugmann, Tina Kretschmer
articles.abstract: Sibling interactions offer countless opportunities to practice empathic behavior and learn about emotional expression of others. In line, various studies have examined links between sibling relationships and empathy. Aiming to provide a systematic overview of this field of research, this meta‐analysis synthesizes studies and evaluates their quality. It provides overall estimates of the strength of associations between empathy and sibling status, quality of the relationship, and presence of a sibling with a disability or illness, and explores sources of heterogeneity in effect sizes. To this end, 118 effect sizes from 26 samples reporting on n = 6665 participants (aged 10 months to 81 years) were included in the quantitative analysis. Additionally, findings of nine qualitative studies with a total of 101 participants were summarized. Sibling relationship quality was positively linked to greater empathy ( r = 0.25), and higher levels of empathy were observed in individuals who have a sibling with a disability or illness ( r = 0.10). Only children did not differ in empathy, which suggests that siblings are just one of many pathways that benefit empathy development. Overall, the field would benefit from more longitudinal studies and studies that include broader family dynamics to capture the complexity of early social development.

articles.title: Spillover and Crossover Effects of Financial Stress in Romantic Dyads: A Daily Diary Study
articles.authors: Zhongchi Li, Gregory D. Webster
articles.abstract: Financial stress can strain romantic relations through stress spillover (affecting oneself) and crossover (affecting one's partner). This study investigated how financial stress influences relationship stress and the role of dyadic coping strategies. Eighty‐four unmarried US couples ( N = 168 respondents) completed a one‐time baseline assessment and a 7‐day daily diary reporting financial stress, relationship stress, and perceived dyadic coping. Multilevel modeling showed financial stress significantly predicted both one's own and one's partner's relationship stress at baseline. Emotion‐focused dyadic coping (providing support, reassurance) buffered this association, whereas problem‐focused coping had no buffering effect and may even worsen stress spillover. Daily analyses revealed that financial stress and relationship stress covary over time, especially for couples with high baseline relationship stress. These findings underscore the protective role of emotion‐focused dyadic coping in managing immediate relational strain due to financial stress, suggesting the need for targeted interventions to foster relationship resilience in financially vulnerable couples.

articles.title: No Validity Without Reliability: Measurement in Relationship Science, 1994–2024
articles.authors: Gregory D. Webster, Soo Yeon Park, Zhongchi Li, Amy Pezoldt, Ashley N. Krause, Anaïs Ortiz, Eva A. García Ferrés
articles.abstract: Measurement reliability is necessary for validity and foundational to theory, inference, and cumulative knowledge in relationship science, yet concerns about questionable measurement practices persist. We examined long‐term trends in measurement reliability and reporting practices across 482 empirical articles published in three leading relationship‐focused journals ( JPSP: IRGP , JSPR , and PR ) in 1994, 2004, 2014, and 2024. Using multilevel models to account for measures nested within studies nested within articles, we assessed change over time and journal differences in internal consistency reliability, scale length, citation age of measures, sample size, sample items, and use of ad‐hoc and single‐item measures. Results revealed steady increases in internal consistency reliability (driven by mean inter‐item correlation increases), alongside accelerating growth in sample sizes and a marked decline in ad‐hoc measures after the mid‐2000s. At the same time, authors increasingly relied on older measures, and trends in scale length, single‐item usage, and sample‐item inclusion varied by journal. Despite gains in reliability, validity reporting remained rare. These findings document meaningful progress in some aspects of measurement practice while underscoring the continued neglect of validity reporting. We conclude with recommendations for researchers, reviewers, and editors aimed at strengthening measurement reporting and cumulative progress in relationship science.

articles.title: Worldviews and public attitudes toward gene-edited foods in Japan
articles.authors: Tomiko Yamaguchi, Ildeung Na
articles.abstract: This study examines public attitudes toward gene-edited foods in Japan, focusing on how underlying worldviews shape these responses. Drawing on a national survey and a latent class segmentation model based on 23 worldview variables, we identify four distinct segments: Communitarian, Environmentalist, Governmentalist, and Individualist. The findings indicate modest rather than sharply polarized differences in attitudes, with the Communitarian and Environmentalist segments expressing greater caution than the Governmentalist and Individualist segments. Across all four segments, gene-edited foods are broadly perceived as unnatural, yet support for commercialization remains comparatively high, suggesting that perceptions of unnaturalness do not necessarily translate into strong opposition to commercialization. This pattern suggests that evaluations of gene-edited foods are shaped by multiple normative considerations, in which moral or symbolic concerns coexist with pragmatic judgments about societal benefits and technological governance. These findings suggest that similar levels of support or skepticism can emerge from differing normative orientations.

articles.title: Beyond Factual Correction: Integrating Meta-Cognitive Deficits Into the Risk Information Seeking and Processing Model to Address HPV Misperception
articles.authors: Yuchen Wang, Yuan Zhong
articles.abstract: Overconfidence, explained by the Dunning–Kruger effect (DKE), hinders engagement with corrective health information. Integrating the DKE with Risk Information Seeking and Processing (RISP) model, a 2 (meta-cognitive vs. informational intervention) × 2 (simple rebuttal vs. factual elaboration) experiment examined human papillomavirus misperceptions. Results show that meta-cognitive interventions limited subjective knowledge, effectively boosting information insufficiency. Conversely, informational inoculation increased subjective knowledge, inadvertently suppressing the insufficiency gap essential for motivation. Path modeling confirmed that information insufficiency predicts seeking and preventive intentions. We demonstrate that overcoming overconfidence requires recalibrating knowledge perceptions rather than merely providing facts, establishing meta-cognition as a contingent condition for RISP.

articles.title: A Causal Inference on the Effects of Attention to Media Content About Autonomous Vehicles in the Influence of Presumed Media Influence Model
articles.authors: Tong Jee Goh, Hongjie Tang, Shirley S. Ho
articles.abstract: Applying the influence of presumed media influence model into an autonomous vehicle (AV) context, this study examines how media viewers’ attention to content about risks and benefits of AVs affects their presumptions of influence of the content on others, perceptions of trustworthiness of the technology, and intention to ride in AVs. Through cross-lagged analyses of two-wave panel data (n wave1 = 1,306; n wave2 = 650), this study found causal evidence for the projection effect and impersonal impact. Notably, this study also found causal evidence for the consonance effect: viewers perceiving trustworthiness of AVs after developing intention to ride in AVs.

articles.title: Once Upon a Genome: A Content Analysis of Narratives and Narrativity in News About Genomic Research
articles.authors: Helena Bilandzic, Susanne Kinnebrock, Markus Schug, Theresa Engstler
articles.abstract: This content analysis investigates the functions and types of narratives in German science news about genomic research as well as their degree of narrativity. The results show that nearly half of all articles contained at least one narrative. They were used predominantly to corroborate scientific findings. Narratives about the research process were most common, followed by narratives about researchers and personal fates of affected individuals. Personal-fate narratives displayed the highest levels of narrativity, research-process narratives the lowest. The findings highlight the value of a differentiated approach to studying narratives in science communication.

articles.title: Humilitainment 2.0: Platformed Crime Entertainment and Digital Carcerality on YouTube
articles.authors: Krysten Stein
articles.abstract: Reality-based crime television has long shaped public understandings of policing, crime, and punishment by turning law enforcement encounters into consumable spectacle. As these narratives migrate into engagement-driven platform infrastructures, where recommendation systems and interactive features reshape how policing media is packaged, encountered, and monetized, their cultural impact is reconfigured. This article examines COPSTV, the official YouTube continuation of COPS , as platformed crime entertainment structured for visibility and circulation. Drawing on a thematic analysis of 200 highly viewed COPSTV videos, I identify three interrelated patterns: the packaging of policing encounters for visibility through sensationalized titles, rapid escalation, and spectacle-oriented narrative sequencing; recurring representations that glorify law enforcement, individualize criminality, criminalize mental health crises, and normalize police violence; and the conversion of public humiliation into a platformed strategy of engagement. I argue that YouTube’s recommendation infrastructure may contribute to the amplification of punitive narratives by increasing the visibility of highly engaging policing content, positioning viewers for participatory judgment while crowding out structural critique. Situating COPSTV within scholarship on platform governance, media convergence, and digital carcerality, the article shows how platform dynamics render coercion and degradation highly visible, clickable, and economically self-reinforcing.

articles.title: Antecedents of Disclosure: What Transparency Measures Social Media Users in the United States Want From Paid Political Influencers
articles.authors: Martin J. Riedl, Benjamin D. Horne, Matthew J. A. Craig, Michael R. Kotowski, Catherine A. Luther
articles.abstract: At the heels of the 2024 U.S. presidential election, public attention turned to the role social media influencers played in Donald J. Trump’s decisive win. In the United States, unlike influencers promoting commercial brands, political influencers – that is, social media influencers who associate themselves with political causes – are not required to disclose whether they got paid in exchange for promoting a political organization, party, or campaign. Through a survey of U.S. social media users ( n = 906), this study explores people’s attitudes toward paid political influencer disclosure. We find that political partisanship impacts support for disclosure: being more conservative is connected to lessened support for disclosure, yet disclosure is of strong bipartisan concern regardless. Our study documents that social media users who care for authenticity – a core currency in influencer ecosystems running on parasocial relationships – also exhibit higher support for disclosure. Yet, at the same time, caveating this empirical relationship between authenticity and disclosure, we also found that those who consumed more political influencer content exhibited lower support for disclosure, pinpointing the normalization of a digital ecology replete with sponsored content. Our study has implications for the broader political communication ecology: As transparency for paid political influencer activities emerges as a topic of public concern, platforms and regulators should advance efforts that provide disclosure about paid political influencer activities to social media users.

articles.title: “Turns Out My Paternal Grandmother has 16% Native Blood”: Racialized DNA, Race Destabilization, and Digital Race-(re)making on Social Media
articles.authors: Yukun Yang, Meredith D. Clark
articles.abstract: This study explores an online phenomenon that we conceptualize as “digital race (re)-making.” In the context of genetic ancestry test discourses, we found digital race (re)-making a sequential four-stage race-making process where users (a) authenticate their previously identified racial identity, (b) destabilize the previous race by incorporating DNA test results, (c) negotiate potential conflict between their previous racial identity and the DNA-inferred race, and (d) utilize social media to affirm and contest their negotiation. Employing multi-round discourse analysis on 466 self-disclosing narratives on the subreddit r/23andMe, we explore the semiotics, strategies, and signifiers that users deployed to discursively disrupt their previously identified racial identity and to create and compose their newly constructed racial identity under the premise of genetic race. By surfacing such a new online racial formation process, we argue that digital platforms actively shape the ways race is re-constructed, re-contested, and re-configured. We also discuss how such a process repudiates the classical identity formation model and how it extends racial socialization theory to the digital enclaves, and how such self-discovery comes with emotional cost.

articles.title: Social Robots and the Dialectics of Presence and Absence
articles.authors: Autumn Edwards, Chad Edwards, Bryan Abendschein
articles.abstract: Social robots function as embodied social media, structuring interaction by simultaneously acting as social agents and mediating technologies. This study examines how 103 young adult participants engaged with zoomorphic social robots in initial encounters, revealing dialectical tensions between presence and absence, connection and disconnection, and realism and artificiality. Drawing from relational dialectics theory (RDT) and semiotics, we frame social robots within a plural communication ontology—operating both as communicative partners and as structuring media that regulate relational expectations. Findings indicate that while social robots facilitate engagement, their enacted affordances also constrain interaction, exposing the limits of artificial presence. Like social media platforms, these robots curate sociality, fostering immersion while highlighting mediation. By conceptualizing social robots as communicative infrastructures, this study advances research on human–machine communication and technological mediation, illustrating how social robots shape social connection through structured engagement and interactive constraints.
